[
  {
    "n": 1,
    "kind": "Example",
    "title": "Standard Input and Output Operations",
    "source": "Lab 1",
    "statement": "Read a user name using gets and evaluate its safety compared to safer alternatives for reading from standard input. Declare strings as literals and character arrays, read and write floats and hexadecimal numbers, use formatted input, and convert between strings and integers."
  },
  {
    "n": 2,
    "kind": "Task",
    "title": "Variable Declarations and Value Limits",
    "source": "Lab 1",
    "statement": "Create a program named ex1.c that declares integer, unsigned short integer, signed long int, float, and double variables. Assign maximum possible values to each variable, print their sizes and values, and write a script ex1.sh to run the program."
  },
  {
    "n": 3,
    "kind": "Task",
    "title": "Character by Character String Reversal",
    "source": "Lab 1",
    "statement": "Write a program named ex2.c that asks the user to type a string character-by-character until a dot or Enter key is entered, supporting up to 256 characters. Print the reversed string enclosed in double quotation marks, and write a script ex2.sh to run the program."
  },
  {
    "n": 4,
    "kind": "Task",
    "title": "Numeral System Base Conversion",
    "source": "Lab 1",
    "statement": "Implement a function convert that converts a given non-negative number from a source numeral system to a target system, where both base specifiers are in the range 2 to 10. Write a program ex3.c that reads the input values and prints the converted number or an error message without using arrays, structures, or pointers, accompanied by a runner script ex3.sh."
  },
  {
    "n": 5,
    "kind": "Task",
    "title": "Character Frequency Counting",
    "source": "Lab 1",
    "statement": "Write a function count that returns the occurrences of a character in a string, and a function countAll that prints occurrences of each character in a case-insensitive manner. Implement a program ex4.c that accepts a command-line string without using arrays, structures, or pointers, and provide an accompanying runner script ex4.sh."
  },
  {
    "n": 6,
    "kind": "Task",
    "title": "Iterative Tribonacci Sequence Calculation",
    "source": "Lab 1",
    "statement": "Write a function tribonacci that calculates the n-th value of the Tribonacci sequence for n between 0 and 37 without using arrays or recursion. Write a program ex5.c that calls this function with arguments 4 and 36, prints the results to standard output, and submit an ex5.sh script to compile and run it."
  },
  {
    "n": 7,
    "kind": "Task",
    "title": "Asterisk Geometric Pattern Printing",
    "source": "Lab 1",
    "statement": "Write a program that prints specified geometric patterns of asterisks to the console, including increasing triangles, decreasing triangles, and rectangular blocks."
  },
  {
    "n": 8,
    "kind": "Task",
    "title": "Variable Naming Rules and Identifiers",
    "source": "Tutorial 1",
    "statement": "Determine whether a variable name can start with a number or typographical symbols such as hash, asterisk, or underscore. Provide an example of an invalid variable name in C and explain why it is rejected by the compiler."
  },
  {
    "n": 9,
    "kind": "Task",
    "title": "Data Type Memory Sizes and Conversions",
    "source": "Tutorial 1",
    "statement": "List at least three primitive data types in C and determine how much memory each requires. Discuss the limitations, truncation risks, and casting requirements when substituting one data type for another, and determine whether type names can serve as variable identifiers."
  },
  {
    "n": 10,
    "kind": "Task",
    "title": "Standard Program Structural Sections",
    "source": "Tutorial 1",
    "statement": "Describe the structure of a standard C program across documentation, link, definition, global declaration, main function, and subprogram sections. Identify which sections are strictly mandatory and which are optional."
  },
  {
    "n": 11,
    "kind": "Task",
    "title": "Variable Scope and Parameter Types",
    "source": "Tutorial 1",
    "statement": "Define program scope and distinguish between global variables, local variables, and formal parameters. Explain their declaration locations and demonstrate accessibility rules using an illustrative multi-function code example."
  },
  {
    "n": 12,
    "kind": "Task",
    "title": "Standard Input Methods and Buffer Safety",
    "source": "Tutorial 1",
    "statement": "Explain the various methods available to supply input to a C program, including command-line arguments, gets, scanf, getline, and fgets. Compare their relative safety regarding buffer overflow vulnerabilities and cross-platform portability."
  },
  {
    "n": 13,
    "kind": "Task",
    "title": "Standard Output Functions and Formatting",
    "source": "Tutorial 1",
    "statement": "Explain how to produce screen output in a C program using puts, fputs, and the printf family of functions. Describe the syntactic differences and formatting capabilities provided by each approach."
  },
  {
    "n": 14,
    "kind": "Task",
    "title": "Call by Value Versus Call by Reference",
    "source": "Tutorial 1",
    "statement": "Contrast passing function arguments by value with passing them by reference. Explain how memory addresses and values are handled in each case, providing code examples to demonstrate whether caller arguments are modified."
  }
]
